title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act): original Official Journal text of the articles and annexes (reproduction, version 2024-08-01)
container: GitHub repository bojkovski-cpu/ai-act-annotated, files src/data/articles_en.json and src/data/annexes_en.json, commit 410bd77 (2026-05-19). Unofficial reproduction of the OJ text, used because EUR-Lex was blocked. It shows the text before the 2026 Omnibus amendments.

claims.claim: The AI Act was published in the Official Journal on 12 July 2024 (OJ L, 2024/1689).
claims.quote: (Artificial Intelligence Act) ( OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj )

claims.claim: As originally adopted, Article 113 made the AI Act generally applicable from 2 August 2026 and applied Chapters I and II from 2 February 2025. Chapter I includes the Article 4 AI-literacy duty and Chapter II the Article 5 prohibitions.
claims.quote: It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025;

claims.claim: As originally adopted, Article 113 applied the notified-body, GPAI (Chapter V), governance and penalties provisions from 2 August 2025.
claims.quote: (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101;

claims.claim: As originally adopted, Article 113 applied Article 6(1) (high-risk AI in Annex I products) and its obligations from 2 August 2027.
claims.quote: (c) Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations in this Regulation shall apply from 2 August 2027.

claims.claim: The original Article 4 required providers and deployers to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff.
claims.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf

claims.claim: Under Article 6(1), the first condition for high-risk status is that the AI system is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Annex I legislation.
claims.quote: the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I;

claims.claim: Under Article 6(1)(b), the second condition is that the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation.
claims.quote: the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment

claims.claim: Under Article 6(2), the AI systems listed in Annex III are also high-risk.
claims.quote: In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk.

claims.claim: Article 50(1) requires providers to design AI systems that interact directly with people so that those people are told they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious.
claims.quote: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious

claims.claim: Article 50(2) requires providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark the outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way.
claims.quote: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

claims.claim: The Article 50(2) marking duty does not apply to assistive editing functions, or where the system does not substantially alter the deployer's input.
claims.quote: This obligation shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof

claims.claim: As published in 2024, Annex I lists 20 Union harmonisation acts: items 1-12 in Section A (New Legislative Framework, with item 6 the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU) and items 13-20 in Section B. Full-text inspection found that the Low Voltage Directive 2014/35/EU is absent, and the EMC Directive 2014/30/EU appears only inside the title of item 20.
claims.quote: Section A. List of Union harmonisation legislation based on the New Legislative Framework

claims.claim: Annex III lists eight high-risk areas: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education; employment; essential services; law enforcement; migration and border control; and justice and democratic processes. Full-text inspection found no area covering equipment repair or diagnostics.
claims.quote: High-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) are the AI systems listed in any of the following areas:

claims.claim: Annex III point 4(b) covers AI used in employment relationships to monitor and evaluate workers' performance and behaviour.
claims.quote: to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.

authors: Publications Office of the European Union
title: Rules for trustworthy artificial intelligence in the EU (EUR-Lex summary of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

claims.claim: Before the 2026 Omnibus, the EUR-Lex summary said the high-risk rules would apply from 2 August 2026 or 2 August 2027.
claims.quote: Most provisions – in particular those governing high-risk AI systems – will only start to apply from 2 August 2026 or 2 August 2027.

claims.claim: The AI Act's governance bodies have been active since 2 August 2025.
claims.quote: The regulation sets up several governing bodies active from 2 August 2025

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
container: Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2026/1744
publisher: EUR-Lex, Publications Office of the European Union

claims.claim: The Digital Omnibus on AI was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026. It amends the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230.
claims.quote: of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)

claims.claim: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026.
claims.quote: published in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJ L, 2026/1744) on 24 July 2026

claims.claim: The Omnibus sets the Chapter III high-risk rules to apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III (Article 6(2)) systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I (Article 6(1)) systems.
claims.quote: set to 2 December 2027 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, and to 2 August 2028 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I

authors: Publications Office of the European Union
title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, consolidated text 02024R1689-20260727 (incorporating Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)

claims.claim: As amended, Article 4 requires providers and deployers to take measures that support the development of AI literacy among their staff.
claims.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf

claims.claim: As amended, Article 4 requires the Commission and the Member States to support providers and deployers, especially SMEs, in meeting the AI-literacy obligation.
claims.quote: The Commission and the Member States shall support and facilitate the efforts of providers and deployers of AI systems, in particular SMEs, in fulfilling their obligation under paragraph 1 of this Article

claims.claim: For high-risk AI in products covered by Annex I Section B legislation, only Article 6(1), the new Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 apply.
claims.quote: only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 shall apply.

claims.claim: Search-result text says that third-party assessment required only for non-health-and-safety risks, such as radio spectrum or EMI, does not satisfy Article 6(1)(b). The snippet could not be pinned to this page with certainty; verify before relying on it.
claims.quote: risks relating to the distribution of radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, shall not be considered as fulfilling the condition in paragraph 1, point (b).

title: Artificial Intelligence: Council and Parliament agree to simplify and streamline rules (Press release 299/26)

claims.claim: The Council presidency and European Parliament negotiators reached a provisional agreement on the AI Omnibus on 7 May 2026.
claims.quote: the Council presidency and European Parliament negotiators reached a provisional agreement on a proposal to streamline certain rules regarding artificial intelligence (AI).

claims.claim: The agreement shortened the grace period for marking AI-generated content, setting a new deadline of 2 December 2026.
claims.quote: reduces the grace period for providers to implement transparency solutions for artificially generated content from 6 months to 3 months, with the new deadline set on 2 December 2026.

claims.claim: The agreement added a prohibited practice covering AI generation of non-consensual sexual or intimate content and CSAM.
claims.quote: prohibiting AI practices regarding the generation of non-consensual sexual and intimate content or child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

title: Artificial Intelligence: Council gives final green light to simplify and streamline rules

claims.claim: The Council gave final approval to the AI Omnibus on 29 June 2026.
claims.quote: the Council gave its final green light on a new regulation aiming to streamline and simplify certain rules regarding artificial intelligence (AI).

claims.claim: The new fixed application dates are 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI embedded in products.
claims.quote: the new application dates would be 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products.

claims.claim: The Omnibus enters into force on the third day after publication in the Official Journal.
claims.quote: The legislative act will be published in the EU's official journal shortly and will enter into force on the third day after this publication.

title: AI Act: EP approves simplification measures and "nudifier" app ban (press release 20260611IPR45207)

claims.claim: In June 2026 the European Parliament approved the AI Act simplification measures together with the ban on 'nudifier' apps.
claims.quote: AI Act: EP approves simplification measures and “nudifier” app ban

title: AI Omnibus enters into force
publisher: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future

claims.claim: The AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026.
claims.quote: On 27 July 2026, the AI Omnibus enters into force across the EU, bringing extended timelines to administrative simplification.

claims.claim: The Commission proposed the Omnibus on 19 November 2025, and political agreement was reached on 7 May 2026.
claims.quote: The legislative proposal was adopted on 19 November 2025, a political agreement was reached on 7 May 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026.

claims.claim: Under the Omnibus, Annex III high-risk rules apply from 2 December 2027, and Annex I product-embedded high-risk rules from 2 August 2028.
claims.quote: High-risk AI systems in Annex III have rules apply starting 2 December 2027, and high-risk AI embedded in physical products (machinery, toys, lifts, etc.) in Annex I have rules apply starting 2 August 2028.

title: Commission starts enforcing AI Act rules and new transparency requirements on 2 August (IP/26/1714)

claims.claim: From 2 August 2026, the AI Office and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act, and the transparency rules started to apply.
claims.quote: From 2 August 2026, the European Commission's AI Office, together with national authorities, will begin enforcing the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act. On the same date, new transparency rules will start to apply.

claims.claim: The Commission's summary of the transparency rules is that chatbots and other interactive AI systems must tell users they are dealing with AI.
claims.quote: Chatbots and other interactive AI systems will have to tell users they are dealing with AI, not a human.

claims.claim: More than 180 organisations had signed the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content.
claims.quote: a first list of more than 180 organisations that have signed the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content

title: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice now available (IP/25/1787)

claims.claim: The AI Office can enforce the GPAI rules one year after they apply for new models, and two years after for models already on the market.
claims.quote: The rules become enforceable by the AI Office of the Commission one year later as regards new models and two years later as regards existing models.

claims.claim: GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027.
claims.quote: Models already on the market before 2 August 2025 must ensure compliance by 2 August 2027.

title: AI Literacy - Questions & Answers
publisher: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future

claims.claim: The Commission states that Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025 and describes the duty in its amended 'support the development' form.
claims.quote: Article 4 of the AI Act entered into application on 2 February 2025, therefore the obligation to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff already applies.

title: Targeted consultation on the draft guidelines for the classification of high-risk artificial intelligence systems
publisher: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future

claims.claim: The Commission's Article 6 guidelines on classifying high-risk systems were still in draft in 2026. The consultation closed on 23 July 2026, and final adoption is expected by the end of 2026.
claims.quote: The consultation deadline was extended to 23 July 2026 and the final guidelines will be adopted by the end of 2026.

title: Directive 2014/35/EU on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits (Low Voltage Directive)

claims.claim: The Low Voltage Directive applies to electrical equipment rated 50 to 1000 V AC or 75 to 1500 V DC.
claims.quote: electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1: AI RMF Core

claims.claim: The core of the AI RMF has four functions, GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, each broken down into categories and subcategories.
claims.quote: The Core is composed of four functions: govern, map, measure, and manage. Each of these high-level functions is broken down into categories and subcategories.

claims.claim: GOVERN is a cross-cutting function that runs through the other three.
claims.quote: Governance is designed to be a cross-cutting function to inform and be infused throughout the other three functions.

claims.claim: MAP establishes the context in which an AI system's risks are framed.
claims.quote: The map function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: AI Risk Management Framework (program page)

claims.claim: The AI RMF is voluntary.
claims.quote: The AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness considerations into the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems.

claims.claim: NIST is revising AI RMF 1.0 as part of the White House AI Action Plan.
claims.quote: The AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan.

claims.claim: NIST released the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) on 26 July 2024.
claims.quote: on July 26, 2024, NIST released NIST-AI-600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile.

claims.quote: On April 7, 2026, NIST released a concept note for an AI RMF Profile on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: NIST AI RMF Playbook

claims.claim: AI RMF 1.0 was released on 26 January 2023. Its Playbook gives suggested actions for achieving each function's outcomes.
claims.quote: The NIST AI RMF Playbook is based on AI RMF 1.0 (released on January 26, 2023), and includes suggested actions, references, and related guidance to achieve the outcomes for the four functions

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1), as described in NIST's July 2024 news release

claims.claim: The Generative AI Profile is organised around 12 risks and just over 200 suggested actions.
claims.quote: the guidance centers on a list of 12 risks and just over 200 actions that developers can take to manage them.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: NIST Artificial Intelligence Update, March 27, 2026

claims.claim: Following America's AI Action Plan, NIST is revising the AI RMF to remove references to misinformation, DEI and climate change.
claims.quote: NIST is in the process of revising the AI Risk Management Framework (RMF) to eliminate references to misinformation, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, and climate change

claims.quote: The Cyber AI Profile centers on three overlapping focus areas: securing AI systems, conducting AI-enabled cyber defense, and thwarting AI-enabled cyberattacks.

claims.claim: NIST planned to release an initial public draft of the Cyber AI Profile in 2026.
claims.quote: develop the initial public draft for release in 2026

claims.quote: It is the policy of the United States to sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.

title: Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan

claims.quote: The Plan identifies over 90 Federal policy actions across three pillars – Accelerating Innovation, Building American AI Infrastructure, and Leading in International Diplomacy and Security

claims.quote: the Attorney General shall establish an AI Litigation Task Force whose sole responsibility shall be to challenge State AI laws inconsistent with the policy set forth in section 2 of this order.

claims.quote: address how State laws requiring alterations to the accurate outputs of AI models can conflict with the requirements of the FTC Act.

title: President Donald J. Trump Unveils National AI Legislative Framework

claims.claim: On 20 March 2026 the Administration issued a national AI legislative framework of recommendations to Congress.

title: Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems (proposed; File No. P264200)

claims.claim: The FTC's proposed July 2026 policy statement says that covertly steering an AI system's outputs can be deceptive under Section 5, even when the steering is done to comply with state law.
claims.quote: Steering an AI system in this manner may deceive consumers in violation of section 5 of the FTC Act, and that is true even if the deceptive steering is done in an effort to comply with State laws.

claims.claim: Comments on the proposed policy statement closed on 31 July 2026.
claims.quote: Comments on the policy statement had to be received on or before Friday, July 31, 2026.

claims.quote: The Order directs appropriate agencies to prioritize the cyber defense of National Security Systems, Department of War information systems, and civilian Federal government information systems.

claims.quote: The act repeals and reenacts provisions with new requirements regarding the use of automated decision-making technology in consequential decisions.

claims.claim: Apart from its Attorney General provisions, SB26-189 takes effect on 1 January 2027.
claims.quote: All other sections of the bill take effect on January 1, 2027, and apply to consequential decisions made on or after the bill's effective date.

title: Directive (EU) 2024/1799 of 13 June 2024 on common rules promoting the repair of goods
publisher: European Commission (Directive on repair of goods page) / EUR-Lex

claims.claim: Member States had to transpose the Repair Directive and apply it from 31 July 2026.
claims.quote: Member States have to transpose it into national rules and apply it from 31 July 2026.

claims.claim: The manufacturer's duty to repair covers only goods subject to the EU reparability requirements listed in Annex II, and only while those requirements apply.
claims.quote: the obligation to repair only applies to products whilst they are subject to the reparability requirements, in particular, the obligation to provide spare parts according to the legal measures listed in Annex II.

claims.claim: For Annex II goods, manufacturers may not use contractual, hardware or software techniques that impede repair.
claims.quote: Manufacturers shall not use any contractual clauses, hardware or software techniques that impede the repair of goods covered by Union legal acts listed in Annex II

claims.claim: Manufacturers that supply spare parts and tools for Annex II goods must offer them at a reasonable price that does not deter repair.
claims.quote: shall offer these spare parts and tools at a reasonable price that does not deter repair.

title: Questions & Answers: Directive on repair of goods (obligation to repair)

claims.quote: amends Annex II to Directive (EU) 2024/1799 of the European Parliament and of the Council promoting the repair of goods to include domestic local space heaters

title: Right to repair: New consumer rights for easy and attractive repairs

title: HB 2963 (2025), Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 121, Diagnosis, Maintenance, and Repair of Certain Digital Electronic Equipment

claims.claim: Texas requires OEMs to make documentation, replacement parts and tools needed for diagnosis and repair available on fair and reasonable terms.
claims.quote: make documentation, replacement parts, and tools, or their equivalents, that are required for the diagnosis, maintenance, or repair of the digital electronic equipment available on fair and reasonable terms

claims.claim: Texas requires availability no later than one year after the equipment is first sold in the state.
claims.quote: not later than one year after the date of the first sale of the equipment in Texas

claims.claim: The Texas law applies only to equipment with a wholesale price of at least $50.
claims.quote: HB 2963 applies only to digital electronic equipment with a wholesale price of at least $50 that is sold to a consumer in Texas.

claims.claim: Only the Texas Attorney General can enforce the law.
claims.quote: The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce the bill's provisions

claims.claim: The Texas Act takes effect on 1 September 2026.
claims.quote: The act takes effect September 1, 2026.

title: ESHB 1483 (2025), chapter 353, Laws of 2025 (right to repair digital electronic products)

claims.claim: From 1 January 2026, Washington requires OEMs to provide parts, tools and documentation on fair and reasonable terms.
claims.quote: Effective January 1, 2026, an original manufacturer shall make available to any independent repair provider or owner on fair and reasonable terms any parts, tools, and documentation

claims.claim: Washington covers digital electronic products first manufactured and first sold or used in the state on or after 1 July 2021.
claims.quote: first manufactured, and first sold or used in Washington, on or after July 1, 2021

claims.claim: Washington restricts parts pairing that prevents installation of otherwise functional replacement parts.
claims.quote: an original manufacturer may not use parts pairing to prevent or inhibit an independent repair provider or an owner from installing or enabling the function of an otherwise functional replacement part

title: Nixing the Fix: An FTC Report to Congress on Repair Restrictions

claims.claim: The FTC's 2021 report to Congress found scant evidence supporting manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions.
claims.quote: there is scant evidence to support manufacturers' justifications for repair restrictions

title: Policy Statement of the Federal Trade Commission on Repair Restrictions Imposed by Manufacturers and Sellers

claims.claim: In July 2021 the FTC committed to prioritising enforcement against unlawful repair restrictions.
claims.quote: committing the agency to focus greater enforcement efforts and resources on unlawful repair restriction practices going forward.

title: FTC Warns Companies to Stop Warranty Practices That Harm Consumers' Right to Repair

claims.claim: In July 2024 FTC staff warned companies against tying warranties to branded parts and against 'warranty void if removed' stickers.
claims.quote: including warnings about tying warranty to use of branded parts and affixing "warranty void if removed" stickers to their products.

title: FTC, States Secure Settlement with Deere & Company, Advancing Farmers' Right to Repair

claims.claim: The July 2026 FTC/states settlement requires Deere, for 10 years, to give farmers and independent repairers the same repair resources as its dealers, including software capabilities.
claims.quote: requires Deere—for the next 10 years and under the supervision of the FTC and plaintiff states—to provide farmers and independent repair providers with the same equipment repair resources, including applicable software capabilities

claims.claim: The resources Deere must provide include fault-code tools, reprogramming and access to technical manuals.
claims.quote: reading, clearing and resetting electronic fault codes; reprogramming of electronic components; restarting a machine following an emissions-related shutdown; and viewing and searching technical manuals

title: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of 23 October 2024 on liability for defective products (Product Liability Directive)
container: Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/2853

claims.claim: The new PLD defines 'product' to include software.
claims.quote: "Product" means all movables, even if integrated into, or inter-connected with, another movable or an immovable; it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software.

claims.claim: Member States must transpose the PLD by 9 December 2026.
claims.quote: Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive by 9 December 2026.

claims.quote: This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026.

title: S. 2937, AI LEAD Act (Aligning Incentives for Leadership, Excellence, and Advancement in Development Act), 119th Congress (introduced September 2025)

claims.claim: The AI LEAD Act (S. 2937) would classify AI systems as products and create a federal product-liability cause of action for AI harms.
claims.quote: The AI LEAD Act classifies AI systems as products and creates a federal cause of action for products liability claims to be brought when an AI system causes harm.

title: S. 2081, Responsible Innovation and Safe Expertise (RISE) Act of 2025, 119th Congress

claims.claim: The RISE Act would give AI developers immunity from civil liability for errors when a learned professional uses their product, conditioned on publishing a model card and model specification.
claims.quote: A developer shall be immune from civil liability for errors generated by an artificial intelligence product when used by a learned professional in the course of providing professional services to a client

claims.claim: The RISE Act's sponsor says professionals, including engineers, keep the duty to verify AI outputs.
claims.quote: they retain the legal duty to exercise due diligence, verify the system's outputs, and stand behind the advice they deliver.

title: 29 CFR 1910.333, Selection and use of work practices (Subpart S, Electrical)
container: 29 CFR Part 1910. Text opened in data/corpus/sections.jsonl of GitHub repo dgrinnell/ehs-regulatory-assistant (ingested from the eCFR versioner API; commit 8c08921, 2026-07-22)
publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, OSHA (text); GitHub corpus by D. Grinnell

claims.claim: OSHA's default rule is that exposed live parts must be de-energised before work on or near them (29 CFR 1910.333(a)(1)).
claims.quote: Live parts to which an employee may be exposed shall be deenergized before the employee works on or near them

claims.claim: OSHA's 50-volt threshold: live parts under 50 V to ground need not be de-energised when there is no increased burn or arc-explosion exposure (29 CFR 1910.333(a)(1)).
claims.quote: Live parts that operate at less than 50 volts to ground need not be deenergized if there will be no increased exposure to electrical burns or to explosion due to electric arcs.

claims.claim: Dangerous stored electrical energy must be released, and capacitors discharged, before equipment is worked on as de-energised (29 CFR 1910.333(b)(2)(ii)(C)).
claims.quote: Stored electric energy which might endanger personnel shall be released. Capacitors shall be discharged and high capacitance elements shall be short-circuited and grounded, if the stored electric energy might endanger personnel.

claims.claim: Capacitors handled while being discharged must be treated as energised.
claims.quote: If the capacitors or associated equipment are handled in meeting this requirement, they shall be treated as energized.

claims.claim: A qualified person must verify the de-energised condition with test equipment (29 CFR 1910.333(b)(2)(iv)(B)).
claims.quote: A qualified person shall use test equipment to test the circuit elements and electrical parts of equipment to which employees will be exposed and shall verify that the circuit elements and equipment parts are deenergized.

title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Articles 5 and 25
container: OJ L 119, 4.5.2016. Text opened in GitHub repo 6022-labs/gdpr-mcp-server, data/v1/articles/art-5 and art-25 (commit 24ef3c2, 2025-11-16), an unofficial reproduction used because EUR-Lex was blocked

claims.claim: GDPR Article 5(1)(c), the data-minimisation principle, limits personal data to what is necessary for the purposes of processing.
claims.quote: (c) adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’);

claims.claim: GDPR Article 25(1), data protection by design, requires appropriate measures such as pseudonymisation that put data-protection principles into effect.
claims.quote: implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, which are designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner

claims.claim: GDPR Article 25(2), data protection by default, allows only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose to be processed.
claims.quote: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed.

claims.claim: The default-minimisation duty covers how much is collected, how far it is processed, how long it is stored and who can access it.
claims.quote: That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility.

title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
container: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 81:1-15 (Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 2018)
publisher: PMLR (PDF opened from the publisher's GitHub repository mlresearch/v81)

claims.claim: Gender Shades found error rates of up to 34.7% for darker-skinned females, against at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned males.
claims.quote: show that darker-skinned females are the most misclassified group (with error rates of up to 34.7%). The maximum error rate for lighter-skinned males is 0.8%.

claims.claim: Gender Shades disaggregates accuracy into intersectional subgroups instead of evaluating single attributes alone.
claims.quote: Instead of evaluating accuracy by gender or skin type alone, accuracy is also examined on 4 intersectional subgroups: darker females, darker males, lighter females, and lighter males.

claims.claim: The authors built a new benchmark balanced by skin type because existing benchmarks were skewed toward lighter-skinned subjects.
claims.quote: introducing a new face dataset composed of 1270 unique individuals that is more phenotypically balanced on the basis of skin type than existing benchmarks.

claims.claim: The authors argue that intersectional error analysis can guide dataset composition and model design.
claims.quote: Intersectional phenotypic and demographic error analysis can help inform methods to improve dataset composition, feature selection, and neural network architectures.

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 2025 edition: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
container: Canonical Markdown source, file 2025/LLM01_PromptInjection.md (the repository README describes it as the previous release)

claims.claim: OWASP 2025 defines prompt injection as user prompts that alter an LLM's behaviour or output in unintended ways.
claims.quote: A Prompt Injection Vulnerability occurs when user prompts alter the LLM’s behavior or output in unintended ways.

claims.claim: OWASP 2025 defines indirect prompt injection as instructions that arrive through external sources such as websites or files.
claims.quote: Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files.

claims.claim: OWASP 2025 says RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate prompt injection.
claims.quote: research shows that they do not fully mitigate prompt injection vulnerabilities.

claims.claim: OWASP 2025 says it is unclear whether any fool-proof prevention exists.
claims.quote: it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention for prompt injection.

claims.claim: OWASP 2025 recommends human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations.
claims.quote: Implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions.

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 (LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection; LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency; LLM07:2026 Misinformation)
container: Canonical Markdown source in 2026/final/ (README.md, LLM00_Preface.md, LLM01_PromptInjection.md, LLM03_ExcessiveAgency.md, LLM07_Misinformation.md)

claims.claim: The 2026 edition of the OWASP LLM Top 10 was published on 4 August 2026 and is now the current release. Prompt injection remains LLM01.
claims.quote: Current release: 2026 — published August 4, 2026.

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 extends prompt injection to inputs from retrieved content, tool output, multimodal content and persistent memory.
claims.quote: input to a large language model (LLM), whether direct user input, retrieved content, tool output, image, audio, or video content, intermediate reasoning, or persistent memory, alters the model's behavior

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 says no single control is sufficient and prescribes defence in depth.
claims.quote: Apply the controls below as defense-in-depth, since no single control is sufficient.

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 recommends keeping credentials and state-changing capability in application code, not in the model, with least privilege for each operation.
claims.quote: Hold credentials and state-change capability in application code, not the model, and grant least privilege per operation.

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 recommends explicit human confirmation before privileged, irreversible or externally visible actions.
claims.quote: Require explicit human confirmation before any privileged, irreversible, or externally visible action

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 adopts the 'Rule of Two': an agent that combines untrusted input, sensitive data and state change needs per-action human approval.
claims.quote: Treat simultaneous access to (A) untrusted input, (B) sensitive data, and (C) state change or external communication as high-risk: any [A,B,C] agent needs per-action human approval

claims.claim: OWASP 2026 (LLM07) defines misinformation as the risk that incorrect but credible output is trusted and acted upon.
claims.quote: The core risk is that the incorrect output is trusted and acted upon.

claims.claim: Excessive Agency rose to third place in the 2026 list because agentic deployments are where the damage is occurring.
claims.quote: Excessive Agency climbed to third, the most consequential move on the list, because the vote and the record agree that agentic deployments are where the damage is landing.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
container: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISec '23); arXiv:2302.12173

claims.claim: Greshake et al. show that indirect prompt injection lets adversaries attack LLM-integrated applications remotely by planting prompts in data likely to be retrieved.
claims.quote: by strategically injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved.

claims.claim: Greshake et al. argue that LLM-integrated applications blur the line between data and instructions.
claims.quote: LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions.

title: llm-security: Compromising LLMs using Indirect Prompt Injection (authors' proof-of-concept repository)

claims.claim: The authors present indirect prompt injection as a new class of vulnerability for language models integrated with applications.
claims.quote: We present a new class of vulnerabilities and impacts stemming from "indirect prompt injection" affecting language models integrated with applications.

claims.claim: The authors conclude that prompt injections can be as powerful as arbitrary code execution.
claims.quote: Prompt injections can be as powerful as arbitrary code execution

claims.claim: The authors conclude that indirect injection is a much more powerful way of delivering injections.
claims.quote: Indirect prompt injections are a new, much more powerful way of delivering injections.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology

claims.claim: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 groups attacks on generative AI into four classes: evasion, poisoning, privacy and misuse.
claims.quote: evasion, poisoning, privacy, and misuse attacks for Generative AI (GenAI) systems

claims.claim: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 has a dedicated section on indirect prompt injection attacks and mitigations.
claims.quote: Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: CSRC Glossary: prompt injection; indirect prompt injection (source: NIST AI 100-2e2025)

claims.claim: NIST defines prompt injection as exploiting the concatenation of untrusted input with a prompt built by a higher-trust party.
claims.quote: An attack which exploits the concatenation of untrusted input with a prompt constructed by a higher-trust party such as the application designer.

claims.claim: NIST defines indirect prompt injection as injection executed through resource control rather than through direct user input.
claims.quote: A type of prompt injection executed through resource control rather than through user-provided input as in a direct prompt injection.

claims.quote: Agent hijacking is a type of indirect prompt injection in which an attacker inserts malicious instructions into data that may be ingested by an AI agent, causing it to take unintended, harmful actions.

claims.quote: AI agent systems are capable of taking autonomous actions that impact real-world systems or environments, and may be susceptible to hijacking, backdoor attacks, and other exploits.

authors: NIST Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)

claims.quote: The Initiative will ensure that the next generation of AI—AI agents capable of autonomous actions—is widely adopted with confidence, can function securely on behalf of its users, and can interoperate smoothly across the digital ecosystem.

title: Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse)

claims.claim: The UK NCSC warns that prompt injection may never be totally mitigated in the way SQL injection can be.
claims.quote: prompt injection attacks against generative artificial intelligence applications may never be totally mitigated in the way SQL injection attacks can be.

claims.claim: The NCSC explains that prompt injection exploits LLMs' inability to distinguish data from instructions.
claims.quote: prompt injection exploits the inability of large language models (LLMs) to distinguish between the two.

title: CaMeL: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (arXiv:2503.18813), research-artifact repository

claims.claim: CaMeL, from Google, Google DeepMind and ETH Zurich, is a design-level defence against prompt injection.
claims.quote: CaMeL: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design

claims.claim: The authors warn that the CaMeL research-artifact implementation may contain bugs and might not be fully secure.
claims.quote: The interpreter implementation likely contains bugs (e.g., it might throw uncaught exceptions and crash) and the implementation might not be fully secure.

title: Ontology of Driving Automation Systems for On-Road Motor Vehicles (BFO-based ontology of SAE J3016)
container: File ontology-autonomous-driving.ttl. Level definitions carry the annotation 'adaptedFrom J3016 APR2021, section 5.1-5.6'. This is a secondary reproduction; SAE's own J3016 page was not reachable.

claims.claim: The ontology draws on SAE J3016 in its June 2018 and April 2021 versions.
claims.quote: SAE document ID: J3016 (JUN2018, APR2021).

claims.claim: Level 0, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.1: the driver performs the entire dynamic driving task (DDT).
claims.quote: the performance by the driver of the entire DDT, even when enhanced by active safety systems

claims.claim: Level 1, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.2: the system performs either lateral or longitudinal control, and the driver does the rest.
claims.quote: the sustained and ODD-specific execution by a driving automation system of either the lateral or the longitudinal vehicle motion control subtask of the DDT (but not both simultaneously)

claims.claim: Level 2, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.3: the system performs both control subtasks, while the driver does object and event detection and response (OEDR) and supervises.
claims.quote: with the expectation that the driver completes the OEDR subtask and supervises the driving automation system

claims.claim: Level 3, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.4: the system performs the entire DDT, but a fallback-ready user must respond to requests to intervene.
claims.quote: the sustained and ODD-specific performance by an ADS of the entire DDT with the expectation that the DDT fallback-ready user is receptive to ADS-issued requests to intervene

claims.claim: Level 4, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.5: the system also performs the fallback within its operational design domain (ODD), with no expectation that a user responds.
claims.quote: the sustained and ODD-specific performance by an ADS of the entire DDT and DDT fallback, without any expectation that a user will respond to a request to intervene

claims.claim: Level 5, per J3016 APR2021 section 5.6: the same as Level 4 but unconditional, with no ODD limit.
claims.quote: the sustained and unconditional (i.e., not ODD-specific) performance by an ADS of the entire DDT and DDT fallback without any expectation that a user will respond to a request to intervene
